content: ORCON, which stands for Operational Research Consultancy, was established in 1974 by a UK-based consultancy firm as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of ambulance services. Over time, this standard was adopted by various countries, including Australia, to assess and improve their ambulance service operations. For the Activation KPI, it is required that all emergency calls have an ambulance dispatched within three minutes of the call being answered. This process typically involves the control room assigning the task to an ambulance crew within one minute, followed by the crew mobilizing and being en route within the next two minutes. The target is to achieve this standard for 95% of all calls. For Category A calls, which are classified as immediately life-threatening emergencies according to the Advanced Medical Priority Dispatch System (AMPDS), the standard requires that 75% of these calls receive an initial response within eight minutes from the time the call is answered. Additionally, 95% of these calls must receive an initial response within 19 minutes. The ambulance service's performance in meeting these targets is expressed as a percentage of calls that comply with these timeframes. Category B calls, on the other hand, are defined by AMPDS as serious but not immediately life-threatening. For these calls, 95% must receive an initial response within 19 minutes. Previously, there was a distinction between urban and rural ambulance services in terms of response time requirements. Urban services were required to respond to 95% of incidents within 14 minutes, while rural services had a 19-minute target. However, as of April 1, 2006, this distinction was eliminated, and all ambulance services, regardless of location, are now held to the same response time standard of 19 minutes for 95% of incidents.
